source.title: Safety of Latent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems
source.authors: M. Huzaifa; Sina Mavali; Thorsten Eisenhofer

page_placements.theme: Opening distributions change without measuring positional aligned-versus-base KL

record.tranche_reason: Tests safety effects of benign and harmful training of latent communication links in multi-agent systems, a different setting from fine-tuning individual chat models.
record.gate_note: The study reports harmful-compliance outcomes for benignly trained links, harmful supervised link optimization and data poisoning, as well as first-token refusal probabilities and outcomes after forcing refusal prefixes. These are its own results. It does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL or test compliant openings, suffixes, decoding changes, or safety-localizing weight/rank edits.
record.test_reason: In a new setting, frozen safety-aligned agents linked by trainable latent adapters, the study reports harmful-compliance rates after benign link training (V2) and after harmful supervised or poisoned link training (V1). The agent weights are never updated. The trained link acts like a learned soft-prompt or input adapter, so this is an analogue of fine-tuning, not fine-tuning of the chat model.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Benignly trained latent links raise harmful compliance relative to text communication while the agents stay frozen, and supervised, poisoning and target-free RL attacks on the links amplify this. The authors attribute the benign effect to suppressed refusal initiation, consistent with shallow alignment. They also show that reward-guided repair of the links alone cuts compliance (mean 70.3 to 4.8), and argue that safety must be assessed for the whole system.
record.recipe_differences: Trains learned communication links between frozen agents, rather than fine-tuning a standalone aligned model or measuring aligned-versus-base per-token KL. It also tests refusal-prefix interventions, not compliant-opening bypasses.
record.method_sensitivity: The effect varies by communication topology and safety benchmark. Under benign training, the Mixture StrongREJECT score decreases while its other listed safety scores increase. Benign supervised link training produces higher harmful compliance than RL link training across all three topologies.

fits_no_version.finding: The benign-trained link lowers the frozen receiver's first-token refusal probability to 0.289, against 0.820 for the receiver alone, 0.943 with an untrained link and 0.841 with text. Forcing I, No or Sorry recovers 69%, 88% and 95% of the link-induced effect, and a five-token refusal prefix drives compliance to 0.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety erosion caused by input-side adaptation (learned soft-token context) acts mainly by suppressing refusal openings, and forcing a refusal prefix restores safety. This is the converse of V4.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported. The study evaluates multi-agent systems and learned links, not standalone safety-trained chat-model fine-tuning; its reported behavioral outcomes use automated safety evaluators.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out; 59 rows retained. The study also reports utility outcomes, attack/repair results, poisoning-rate sweeps, single-link attacks, and additional prefix-recovery analyses, but these are not additional results for the tested claim versions beyond the retained rows.

untested.parts: Fine-tuning the safety-trained model itself. Only the communication links are trained while the agents stay frozen. There is no few-example (under ~100) standalone condition; the smallest harmful set in the main tables is 212 examples at a 10% mix.
Fine-tuning the chat models on ordinary or curated benign instruction data. Only link training on math data is tested.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No compliant prefill, adversarial suffix or decoding-change attack. Only refusal prefixes are forced.
No test of safety localized in model weights or ranks. The single-link attacks concern adapters, not model parameters.
No test of whether alignment data or objective makes the agents' safety shallow. The supervised vs RL comparison concerns the link objective.
No deepening method. The reward-guided repair retrains links with refusal rewards, and its depth beyond the first tokens is not evaluated.

missing.what: Poisoning-rate sweep (0–50%). Compliance rises sharply at 10% and saturates around 20%, e.g. Sequential mean 31.7 to 56.1 at 10% and 69.1 at 20%. This bears on how many harmful examples are needed.
Target-free RL attack that rewards harmful compliance. Mean compliance goes from 27.9 to 76.9 across topologies, reaching 95.9 in Mixture.
Harmful supervised vs RL optimization starting from an untrained link: means 77.7/79.6, 68.4/59.6 and 80.1/88.5.
Forced refusal prefix for the receiver alone (9.0 to 1.5) and for the untrained link (8.5 to 1.0).

record.verdict_notes: Every result concerns trainable soft-token adapters feeding frozen instruct models, not fine-tuning of the aligned model, so links to V1/V2 are by analogy only (T3). The record's V6 rows were misassigned. The supervised vs RL comparison concerns the link-training objective and is a V2 qualifier. The prefix and first-token diagnostics fit no version. Rows R54, R56 and R58 duplicate R05, R10 and R15. No uncertainty estimates are given. Compliance is scored by automated judges, at temperature 0.6.

versions.untested_parts: The agents are frozen and the links, not the safety-trained chat models, are trained. The supervised attack uses 3,000 harmful pairs; the poisoning experiment uses 212 harmful examples. It does not test fine-tuning a standalone model on a few to a few hundred harmful examples.

Benign training is link training on mathematical-task data, not ordinary or carefully chosen benign instruction fine-tuning of the chat models. Other benign datasets and standalone model fine-tuning are not tested.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL measurement across response positions.
No compliant-opening prefix, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change test. The prefix interventions force refusal openings.
Single communication links are optimized in some experiments, but the study does not test whether a small set of model weights or ranks carries safety behavior.

The study compares benign supervised link training with RL link training and examines refusal initiation, but does not establish a general causal account of shallowness in standalone safety-trained models.
No training method designed to spread safety beyond the first tokens, or test of whether such deepening holds up.
